Asroon / Ahangar / 2021–2022

Asroon: redesigning the PLP for pricing clarity

A product-list redesign for a metal marketplace that made size, price, and quality easier to compare.

Company / productAsroon / Ahangar
Timeline[Add project timeline]

Selected image from the original case study.

Overview

Asroon is a one-stop source for business metal needs. In 2022, the business was selling more than 92,000,000 kg of metal online. The product-list page carried a lot of complexity: brands, qualities, sizes, and properties all competed for attention. The redesign focused on making the next useful action easier to see.

Context

In January 2021, the team asked how UX could help increase online sales. I investigated the existing site, followed a purchase flow, reviewed competitors, and looked for friction in the page itself.

Problem

Users struggled to find the product they wanted. Filters were difficult to use, mobile users saw too little information at once, and the existing grouping privileged brands even when customers were looking for a size.

My role and team

I handled discovery, design, and post-launch analysis. The work was collaborative with the CEO, CTO, marketing expert, and technology team.

Discovery and research

I used stakeholder interviews, CRM feedback, competitor benchmarking, desk research, and heuristic evaluation. The findings pointed to four practical problems:

  1. Filters did not give enough feedback about the system state.
  2. Mobile users had to scroll too much to compare products.
  3. Customers were looking for sizes more often than brands.
  4. Too much information arrived before the user had chosen a direction.

Product and design strategy

The redesign reduced the amount of information shown at once and gave the important information more room. It also treated technical performance as part of the experience: the team changed the technology used to load data faster and added analytics events for later iteration.

Final solution

A smaller, more usable filter

Unnecessary filters were removed, while the remaining controls were made more explicit. A loading state helped users understand that the system was responding to their interaction.

A “Top of Market” category

The team added a section near the top of the page for products with the lowest price, strongest quality, or most demand. It gave users a useful starting point before they reached the full table.

Grouping by size

The product list moved from brand-based grouping to size-based grouping. A quick filter made that shift easier to use, especially on mobile.

A more useful mobile table

The mobile version used an accordion pattern so more products could be scanned at once, with details available when the user wanted them.

Results and measurable impact

The conversion rate later moved from approximately 0.8–1% to 2%. The team also invested further in technology, product, and design after the update. The original article notes that analytics goal-setting was not fully accurate at the time, so the result should be read as a directional outcome rather than a perfectly controlled experiment.

Learnings

The best solution did not come from making the page denser. It came from choosing what to foreground, what to defer, and what the customer was actually using as a decision variable.
